subtopic_detail: Monthly lower abdominal pain and difficulty passing urine in a fourteen year old who has never menstruated
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a fourteen year old girl brought by her mother with six months of lower tummy pain that comes on for three or four days about every four weeks and then eases.

For the last two days she has been passing small amounts of urine frequently and this morning could not pass urine at all. She has never had a period. Her breasts and pubic hair developed from about eleven years of age and her height has followed the 75th centile since primary school.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Breast and pubic hair development at Tanner stage 5, smooth suprapubic mass palpable to just below the umbilicus and tender, bladder scan showing 620 mL of retained urine, external genital inspection showing a bulging bluish membrane at the introitus with no visible vaginal opening, no inguinal masses
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative, urine dipstick negative for nitrites and leucocytes, pelvic ultrasound showing a distended vagina filled with echogenic fluid and a normal uterus and both ovaries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Insert an indwelling urinary catheter and refer her for surgical incision of the obstructing membrane under anaesthesia
options.rationale: Obstructed menstrual outflow behind an imperforate hymen is relieved definitively by a planned hymenotomy performed under general anaesthesia by a gynaecologist, with catheterisation first to relieve the retention that brought her in. Surgery is arranged promptly because retained blood distends the vagina and uterus and can reflux into the pelvis. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology

options.text: Aspirate the collection with a wide bore needle in the emergency department and send the fluid for culture and cytology
options.rationale: Needle aspiration decompresses the collection temporarily but leaves the obstruction in place, so it refills and the puncture introduces infection into a closed space, with pyocolpos the feared result. Definitive incision under anaesthesia avoids both problems. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology

options.text: Commence a combined oral contraceptive pill continuously to suppress menstruation and review her symptoms in three months
options.rationale: Hormonal suppression stops further accumulation but does nothing about the blood already trapped behind the obstruction or about the urinary retention it is causing. It has a role only as a temporising measure when definitive surgery must be deferred. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology

options.text: Arrange karyotype and serum testosterone before making any decision about surgical or hormonal management of her symptoms
options.rationale: Karyotype and androgen measurement answer the question posed by absent menses with absent uterus, as in complete androgen insensitivity or Mullerian agenesis, whereas ultrasound here shows a normal uterus and ovaries with an obstructed vagina. Cyclical pain with a visible obstructing membrane is a mechanical problem, not an endocrine one. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis and defer any intervention until the imaging has been formally reported
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is valuable when ultrasound suggests a more complex obstruction such as a transverse vaginal septum or an obstructed hemivagina with a duplicated system, because the surgical approach differs. A bulging membrane visible at the introitus with a normal uterus on ultrasound does not need further imaging before treatment. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Primary amenorrhoea)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Primary amenorrhoea

explanation.summary: An imperforate hymen is the commonest obstructive anomaly of the female genital tract and characteristically presents in early adolescence with cyclical pelvic pain in a girl who has normal secondary sexual development but has never menstruated. Retained menstrual blood distends the vagina and later the uterus, and the enlarging mass compresses the bladder neck to cause frequency and then acute retention, which is often the symptom that brings the girl to hospital. The diagnosis is made by inspecting the introitus, where a bulging bluish membrane is seen, and confirmed with pelvic ultrasound showing a fluid filled vagina above a normal uterus and ovaries. Treatment is surgical incision and drainage under general anaesthesia, and the differentials that must be separated from it are a transverse vaginal septum, which sits higher and needs different surgical planning, and the conditions in which the uterus is absent, where the presentation is amenorrhoea without cyclical pain. Long term outcomes after timely hymenotomy are excellent, although prolonged obstruction is associated with retrograde menstruation and endometriosis.
key_points: Cyclical pain with normal secondary sexual characteristics and no menses suggests obstructed outflow with a functioning uterus.
Urinary frequency then retention is a common presenting feature as the distended vagina compresses the bladder neck.
Inspection of the introitus makes the diagnosis and ultrasound confirms a normal uterus above a fluid filled vagina.
Definitive treatment is hymenotomy under anaesthesia, not needle aspiration, which risks infection of a closed space.
Absent uterus on imaging moves the assessment to karyotype and androgen studies instead.
explanation.pearls: Acute urinary retention in an adolescent girl who has not yet menstruated should prompt inspection of the introitus before any other investigation, because obstructed menstruation is the mechanism in a substantial proportion and the diagnosis is made in seconds at the bedside.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology

subtopic_detail: Fever with myalgia and diarrhoea at twenty eight weeks after eating soft cheese and pre-prepared salad
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar assessing a 31 year old woman at 28 weeks gestation in her first pregnancy who has had three days of fever, aching muscles and loose stools. She feels wretched but has no cough, dysuria or rash.

She went to a friend's baby shower five days ago and ate soft cheese and a pre-prepared coleslaw. She reports normal foetal movements and has had no contractions or vaginal loss. Her antenatal course has been uncomplicated and her first trimester screening was low risk.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 158 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and non tender with fundal height consistent with dates, no uterine activity on palpation, chest clear on auscultation, no renal angle tenderness, no rash, cardiotocograph with normal baseline variability and accelerations and no decelerations
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 14.2 x10^9/L (5.5 to 15.0 in pregnancy), C reactive protein 62 mg/L (less than 5), midstream urine microscopy with no organisms or pyuria, haemoglobin 108 g/L (110 to 140)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Send stool for culture and give oral rehydration advice, with review arranged if she is still febrile in 48 hours
options.rationale: Stool culture has poor sensitivity for this organism because faecal carriage is intermittent and selective media are needed, and waiting 48 hours in a febrile pregnant woman risks foetal infection becoming established. Supportive care alone is appropriate for viral gastroenteritis in a woman who is afebrile and well. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Take blood cultures and start intravenous benzylpenicillin, with gentamicin added after discussion with the physician
options.rationale: A febrile flu like illness with gastrointestinal upset after high risk foods in pregnancy is listeriosis until proven otherwise, blood culture is the test that makes the diagnosis because stool culture is unreliable, and high dose penicillin with an aminoglycoside for synergy is the treatment. Empirical treatment starts before the culture result because transplacental infection causes stillbirth and preterm birth. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Commence oral azithromycin for a presumed atypical respiratory infection and arrange a chest radiograph with abdominal shielding
options.rationale: Atypical pneumonia is a reasonable consideration for fever with myalgia, but she has no cough and a clear chest, and macrolides do not cover the organism that this food history and this illness pattern point towards. Radiography would be indicated if respiratory signs or hypoxia were present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Give a single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone and arrange outpatient review with repeat inflammatory markers in 24 hours
options.rationale: Cephalosporins have no useful activity against Listeria monocytogenes, which is precisely why the organism is a named gap in cephalosporin cover and why ampicillin is added to empirical regimens in pregnancy and in older patients. Choosing this agent would leave the likely pathogen untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Administer intramuscular betamethasone for foetal lung maturation and admit her for observation without antimicrobial therapy
options.rationale: Antenatal corticosteroid is given when preterm birth within seven days is anticipated, and she has no uterine activity, no cervical change and no ruptured membranes. Withholding antibiotics while observing a febrile woman at 28 weeks allows bacteraemia to seed the placenta. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Antenatal corticosteroids)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Antenatal corticosteroids

explanation.summary: Listeriosis is uncommon but pregnant women are around eighteen times more likely than the general population to acquire it, and the maternal illness is deceptively mild, typically fever with myalgia, headache and sometimes diarrhoea, so the diagnosis rests on maintaining suspicion. The organism is acquired from soft and semi soft cheeses, pre-prepared salads and coleslaw, cold cooked chicken, pate, smoked seafood and rockmelon, and it grows at refrigeration temperatures, which is why the food safety advice given in Australian antenatal care focuses on freshly prepared and thoroughly heated foods. Blood culture is the diagnostic test of choice because bacteraemia is present in most pregnancy associated cases while stool culture is insensitive. Treatment is high dose intravenous benzylpenicillin or ampicillin, with gentamicin added for synergy in severe infection, and cephalosporins are ineffective. Untreated maternal infection crosses the placenta and causes miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm labour and early onset neonatal sepsis with granulomatosis infantiseptica, so empirical treatment while cultures are pending is standard.
key_points: Pregnant women have markedly increased susceptibility and typically present with a mild flu like illness rather than severe sepsis.
Blood culture is the diagnostic test; stool culture is unreliable for this organism.
High dose penicillin or ampicillin with gentamicin for synergy is the treatment, and cephalosporins do not cover it.
Refrigerated ready to eat foods including soft cheese, pre-prepared salads, pate and cold cooked chicken are the classic sources.
Transplacental spread causes miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth and early onset neonatal sepsis.
explanation.pearls: A febrile pregnant woman with no localising source should have blood cultures taken and empirical ampicillin or benzylpenicillin started within the hour, because the maternal illness is often mild while the foetal loss rate in untreated pregnancy associated listeriosis approaches one in five.

sources.label: Food Standards Australia New Zealand: Listeria and food safety advice for pregnancy
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Antenatal corticosteroids

subtopic_detail: Pain over the pubic symphysis and posterior pelvis limiting walking at twenty six weeks in an otherwise well pregnancy
stem:
You are the general practitioner providing shared antenatal care to a 29 year old woman at 26 weeks gestation in her second pregnancy. For six weeks she has had pain across the front of her pelvis and over both buttocks that is worst when she turns in bed, climbs stairs or stands on one leg to dress.

She works as a primary school teacher and is now walking with a waddling gait and taking paracetamol most days. Foetal movements are normal and there have been no contractions, no vaginal loss and no urinary symptoms. Her blood pressure and urinalysis at each visit have been unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Tenderness on direct palpation over the pubic symphysis and over both sacroiliac joints, pain reproduced on the active straight leg raise and on the posterior pelvic pain provocation test, full painless range of movement at both hips, no lumbar spine tenderness, normal power and reflexes in both legs with intact perineal sensation, uterus soft and non tender with fundal height consistent with dates
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for protein, nitrites, leucocytes and blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Advise rest from work with avoidance of all weight bearing activity until delivery, and certify her as unfit for duties
options.rationale: Prolonged rest and complete avoidance of loading worsen deconditioning and pain and are explicitly not recommended, and graded activity within pain limits is the goal instead. Workplace modification may well be needed but is tailored rather than delivered as blanket rest. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine and sacroiliac joints, and review her once it has been reported
options.rationale: Imaging is reserved for features suggesting another pathology, such as radicular pain with neurological deficit, saddle anaesthesia, bladder dysfunction, fever or a history of malignancy, none of which are present. Pelvic girdle pain is a clinical diagnosis confirmed by provocation testing. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy

options.text: Refer her to a pelvic health physiotherapist for an individualised exercise program and a pelvic support belt
options.rationale: Pregnancy related pelvic girdle pain responds best to physiotherapy that combines education, activity modification, stabilising exercise and a pelvic support belt, and this has the strongest evidence of any intervention for the condition. Simple analgesia with paracetamol continues alongside, but the referral is the step that changes her function. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy

options.text: Prescribe a short course of a non steroidal anti inflammatory drug at the lowest effective dose for her pelvic pain
options.rationale: Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are avoided in the second half of pregnancy because of the risk of constriction of the ductus arteriosus and of oligohydramnios through reduced foetal renal perfusion. Paracetamol remains the analgesic of choice with physiotherapy as the mainstay. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Book an elective caesarean section at 39 weeks on the grounds that vaginal birth will aggravate her pelvic symptoms
options.rationale: Caesarean section does not improve pelvic girdle pain outcomes and adds surgical morbidity to a woman who already has reduced mobility, so the condition alone is not an indication. Birth planning instead focuses on positioning, avoiding extremes of hip abduction and documenting her comfortable range. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Pregnancy related pelvic girdle pain affects around one in five pregnancies and arises from altered load transfer through the pelvic ring under the influence of increasing mass, changed posture and ligamentous laxity. It is diagnosed clinically by pain located between the iliac crest and the gluteal fold, with or without symphyseal pain, reproduced by provocation tests such as the posterior pelvic pain provocation test and the active straight leg raise, and it is distinguished from lumbar radicular pain by the absence of dermatomal sensory loss, weakness or reflex change. Management is conservative and multimodal, centring on physiotherapy delivered by a clinician experienced in pelvic health, activity modification, a pelvic support belt and paracetamol, with non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs avoided after the first half of pregnancy. Most women improve substantially within three months of birth, and persistent severe symptoms warrant ongoing physiotherapy rather than imaging. Red flags that redirect the assessment include fever, neurological deficit, bladder or bowel dysfunction and pain that is unrelieved by rest.
key_points: Diagnosis is clinical, using pain location plus provocation tests, and imaging is not required.
Physiotherapy with education, stabilising exercise and a support belt is the first line intervention.
Complete rest is counterproductive; graded activity within pain limits is recommended.
Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are avoided after about twenty weeks because of ductal constriction and oligohydramnios.
Neurological deficit, fever or bladder dysfunction move the assessment away from pelvic girdle pain.
explanation.pearls: The active straight leg raise doubles as a treatment guide: if the leg lifts more easily when the examiner compresses the pelvis, a pelvic support belt worn low over the greater trochanters is likely to relieve symptoms.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy
Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews: Interventions for preventing and treating pelvic and back pain in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Severe nipple pain with shallow attachment on day nine postpartum where feeding has not yet been formally assessed
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 27 year old woman nine days after an uncomplicated vaginal birth of her first baby. She describes a stabbing pain each time the baby attaches that eases part way through the feed, and she has started to dread feeds.

Her sister told her the baby has a tongue tie and that it needs cutting. The baby feeds for about fifty minutes each time, ten times a day, and regained birthweight yesterday. There is no breast lump, redness or fever.

data_table.Examination: Both nipples with a wedge shaped compression line and a shallow superficial fissure at the base of the left nipple, no cracks or exudate, breasts soft after feeds with no erythema or focal tenderness, infant with a thin membrane from the floor of the mouth to just behind the tongue tip, tongue elevates to the mid mouth when crying and extends to the lower lip margin, infant alert with moist mucous membranes and normal tone
data_table.Investigations: Infant weight 3420 g today with birthweight 3390 g, eight wet nappies and four yellow stools in the last 24 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer the baby for immediate frenotomy on the basis of the visible membrane and her description of painful attachment
options.rationale: Division is considered only when a restrictive tongue tie is demonstrated to be impairing feeding after a structured feeding assessment, because a visible frenulum is present in many babies who feed without difficulty. Cutting first means a proportion of women keep the pain and lose the chance to fix the attachment. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Australasian College of Physicians: Position statement on ankyloglossia)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Australasian College of Physicians: Position statement on ankyloglossia

options.text: Arrange a structured feeding assessment with a lactation consultant to observe positioning, attachment and milk transfer
options.rationale: Nipple pain with a wedge shaped compression line is the signature of shallow attachment, which is the commonest cause of nipple trauma and is correctable, and an observed feed is the only way to assess positioning, attachment, suck and transfer together. The assessment also determines whether any tongue restriction is functionally significant before irreversible intervention is considered. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Australasian College of Physicians: Position statement on ankyloglossia)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Australasian College of Physicians: Position statement on ankyloglossia

options.text: Prescribe topical miconazole gel for the infant and an antifungal cream for both nipples after each feed for two weeks
options.rationale: Candidal nipple infection causes burning pain that persists after the feed and is often accompanied by oral plaques or a persistent nappy rash, whereas pain that occurs on attachment and eases during the feed is mechanical. Treating for thrush here would delay the correction of attachment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Advise expressing and giving all feeds by bottle for two weeks so that the nipple fissure has a chance to heal fully
options.rationale: Two weeks of exclusive expressing at this stage risks supply and often ends direct breastfeeding altogether, and it leaves the attachment problem uncorrected for when feeds resume. Short term expressing has a place only when trauma is so severe that feeding cannot continue while attachment is being corrected. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Nipple pain)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Nipple pain

options.text: Commence oral domperidone to increase her supply and recommend she offer formula top ups after each breastfeed
options.rationale: Her baby has regained birthweight with eight wet nappies a day, so supply is adequate and there is no indication for a galactagogue or for supplementation. Domperidone also carries a dose related risk of QT prolongation and is used only for demonstrated low supply after feeding technique has been optimised. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

explanation.summary: Nipple pain is the commonest reason women stop breastfeeding in the first fortnight, and the great majority of cases are caused by shallow attachment rather than by infection or tongue tie. The history that points to a mechanical cause is pain at the moment of attachment that eases as the feed progresses, and the examination finding is a compressed, wedge shaped or blanched nipple after the feed with fissuring at the base. Candidal infection by contrast causes burning that persists or worsens after feeds, while bacterial infection produces a weeping fissure with surrounding erythema. Ankyloglossia is common, present in up to ten per cent of infants, but only a minority of visible ties restrict function, so Australian guidance requires a structured feeding assessment demonstrating impaired function before frenotomy is offered. Early skilled support preserves breastfeeding: most women whose attachment is corrected report a substantial reduction in pain within days without any procedure on the baby.
key_points: Pain at attachment that eases during the feed, with a wedge shaped compression line, indicates shallow attachment.
Burning pain persisting after feeds with oral plaques suggests candida, a different problem with a different treatment.
A visible frenulum is common and does not itself indicate frenotomy; functional restriction must be demonstrated.
A structured feeding assessment observing positioning, attachment and transfer is the pivotal investigation.
Adequate weight gain and wet nappies exclude low supply and remove any indication for galactagogues or top ups.
explanation.pearls: Assess the tongue functionally rather than by appearance: an infant who can elevate the tongue to the mid mouth with the jaw open and extend it past the lower gum has adequate mobility, and pain in that setting is almost always attachment related.

sources.label: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Australasian College of Physicians: Position statement on ankyloglossia

subtopic_detail: Intrauterine device visible below the gestational sac on ultrasound at seven weeks in a continuing pregnancy
stem:
You are the doctor in an early pregnancy assessment clinic seeing a 33 year old woman with a positive pregnancy test who has a copper intrauterine device in place, inserted two years ago. She has two children and wishes to continue this pregnancy.

She has had light spotting for two days but no pain, fever or discharge. She could not feel her threads when she checked last month and did not seek review at the time.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender, speculum examination showing a closed cervix with threads visible at the external os and a small amount of old blood in the vagina, uterus consistent with dates on bimanual examination, no adnexal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound showing a single intrauterine gestational sac with a foetal pole and cardiac activity at 7 weeks 1 day, the intrauterine device lying in the lower uterine cavity below the gestational sac, no adnexal mass, no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Give a prophylactic course of oral doxycycline and defer any decision about the device until the second trimester scan
options.rationale: Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy after the first trimester because of effects on developing teeth and bone, and prophylactic antibiotics do not reduce the obstetric risks of a retained device. Deferring past the first trimester also forfeits the window in which removal is easiest and most beneficial. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Leave the device in place and arrange serial ultrasound surveillance for chorioamnionitis through the second trimester
options.rationale: Retention is associated with roughly double the rate of second trimester loss, preterm birth and intrauterine infection, and ultrasound surveillance cannot prevent those outcomes. Leaving the device is the fallback when the threads are not visible and removal would require instrumentation of the uterus. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Intrauterine contraception)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Intrauterine contraception

options.text: Arrange hysteroscopic retrieval of the device under general anaesthesia on the next available elective operating list
options.rationale: Hysteroscopy in an ongoing pregnancy distends the cavity with fluid and carries a far higher risk of membrane rupture and pregnancy loss than simple traction on visible threads. It is not used for device retrieval in a continuing pregnancy. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Intrauterine contraception)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Intrauterine contraception

options.text: Remove the device now by gentle traction on the visible threads, having counselled her about the small risk of miscarriage
options.rationale: When the threads are visible and the device lies below the gestational sac, early removal roughly halves the rates of miscarriage, preterm birth and chorioamnionitis compared with leaving it in situ, so removal is recommended despite a small immediate procedural risk. The conversation covers that a proportion of women miscarry around the time of removal even though the overall risk is lower with removal. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Intrauterine contraception)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Intrauterine contraception

options.text: Refer her for uterine artery Doppler assessment at twelve weeks and manage the pregnancy as high risk without intervention
options.rationale: Uterine artery Doppler is used to stratify risk of pre-eclampsia and foetal growth restriction and says nothing about the risks created by a retained intrauterine device. Labelling the pregnancy high risk without acting on the modifiable factor leaves the actual hazard untouched. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Intrauterine contraception)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Intrauterine contraception

explanation.summary: Pregnancy with an intrauterine device in situ is uncommon but carries substantially increased risks of miscarriage, second trimester loss, chorioamnionitis and preterm birth if the device remains through the pregnancy. The first step in any woman with a positive test and a device in place is to establish the location of the pregnancy, because the proportion of pregnancies that are ectopic is higher in device users even though the absolute risk of ectopic pregnancy is lower than in women using no contraception. Once an intrauterine pregnancy is confirmed and the woman wishes to continue, removal is recommended when the threads are visible, ideally in the first trimester, and this reduces adverse outcomes by roughly half compared with retention. If the threads are not visible, blind instrumentation is avoided and the device is left in place with counselling about the elevated risks and the need to seek review for fever, pain or bleeding. The device is documented in the notes so that it is sought at delivery and after the placenta is examined.
key_points: Confirm the location of the pregnancy first, since device users who conceive have a higher proportion of ectopic pregnancies.
With visible threads and a continuing intrauterine pregnancy, early removal halves the risks of loss, preterm birth and infection.
If the threads are not visible, the device is left in place rather than blindly instrumented.
Hysteroscopic retrieval is not used in a continuing pregnancy because of the risk of membrane rupture.
Document the retained device so that it is looked for at birth and with the placenta.
explanation.pearls: The single practical determinant of management is whether the threads are visible at the external os: visible threads mean gentle traction in clinic, and absent threads mean counselling and retention, with no role for blind hooks or hysteroscopy in a wanted ongoing pregnancy.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Intrauterine contraception
